title: Floral ceramic dish — course cover
text:
Floral ceramic dish — course cover | Form & Surface
A shallow circular ceramic dish has a glossy white surface and a narrow red-edged rim. A double red circle encloses the central flower group.

title: Floral ceramic dish — course cover
text:
Floral ceramic dish — course cover | Composition
The centre presents the flowers upright. The outer groups rotate around it. The circular frame makes the same floral vocabulary work at two scales: a small central arrangement and an enlarged surrounding repeat.

title: Floral ceramic dish — course cover
text:
Floral ceramic dish — course cover | Colour & Motifs
Two upright red flowers with dark blue bases fill the centre, among green leaves and slender flowering stems. Three large blue-and-red flower groups turn around the outer field. Green leaves, looping red stems and small rosettes fill the spaces between them.

title: Floral ceramic dish — course cover
text:
Floral ceramic dish — course cover | Slide Context
Course reading: Under ‘Ebb and Flow: Art and Globalism of Oceanic Networks,’ the upper-left dish is grouped with the lower-left floral fabric (m1-p01-r02) and the trader-and-horses stone relief at right (m1-p01-r03). Flowers recur across ceramic and textile, while the relief supplies the people and traded animals that make the contact argument concrete. Together the three media introduce the circulation of goods, designs and artisanal knowledge through trade. Slides 2–3 develop that argument through the Paigah Tombs and the Coromandel kalamkari hanging, connecting ornament to human interaction and the movement of making practices.

title: Floral fabric detail — course cover

Floral fabric detail — course cover | Field & Border Organization
Two decorated panels flank a pale vertical strip. Red outer edges enclose cream floral borders, dark green upper fields and red lower fields. The borders follow the panels’ curved and angled edges.

Still Life with Lobster and Fruit | Slide Context
### Module 4, slide 5

**Heading context:** New ways of knowing, materiality, and trade networks

Course reading: The VOC ship model and lavish lobster-and-fruit still life connect transport with the consumption and display of goods. Between Amsterdam and Asia develops into a discussion of materiality and trade. The painted table is therefore read through economic circulation as well as arrangement, colour and texture.

title: Akbar and Adham Khan
text:
Akbar and Adham Khan | Composition
A palace terrace occupies the upper half. A falling inverted figure connects it to a crowded lower court. Horizontal text bands divide the image without stopping the downward narrative movement.

title: Akbar and Adham Khan
text:
Akbar and Adham Khan | Perspective Convention
Tilted balconies, stacked interiors and a steep stairway expose several spaces at once. This is narrative spatial organization, not an unsuccessful single-point perspective.

title: Akbar and Adham Khan
text:
Akbar and Adham Khan | Figural Style
Robes, turbans and contrasting coloured garments distinguish court figures. Gesture and falling bodies communicate conflict.

title: Akbar and Adham Khan
text:
Akbar and Adham Khan | Text–Image Relationship
Calligraphy runs through upper and lower registers and along the bottom margin.

title: Akbar and Adham Khan
text:
Akbar and Adham Khan | Motifs & Hidden Details
Tiny birds occupy the upper-right architectural compartment. Patterned carpets and wall tiles distinguish courtly surfaces.

title: Akbar and Adham Khan

### Module 5, slide 4

**Heading context:** Sartorial choices and legitimacy of a ruler

Course reading: Akbar and Adham Khan is used to discuss sartorial choices and a ruler’s legitimacy after the muslin sequence. Clothing operates as a political visual language, not simply surface pattern. The following Christian-subject paintings extend the enquiry into the Mughal court’s selective use of different visual resources.

The sheet is split vertically into two goddess images. Kali at left has four arms, loose dark hair, a garland of heads, a blade and severed head, with reclining bodies below. ### Module 6, slide 3

**Heading context:** Indigenous Printing in the Indian subcontinent

Course reading: The unfinished Pedana woodblocks and finished Polavaram cotton connect a carved matrix to textile printing. This precedes the European Saint Sebastian block-and-impression pair. The sequence compares a printing principle across supports and uses, while keeping the specific practices distinct.

**Same slide:** [European Print and Indian Bazaar](<european-print-and-indian-bazaar.md>), [Kalamkari printed cotton — Polavaram](<kalamkari-printed-cotton-polavaram.md>), [Unfinished textile woodblocks — Pedana](<unfinished-textile-woodblocks-pedana.md>).

text:
Chromolithography and hand-colouring | Distinctions
**Exam distractor:** “Any coloured print is a chromolithograph, including one coloured by hand after printing.”

**Why it is wrong:** Chromolithography prints colour through lithographic operations. Hand-colouring adds colour after an impression is printed; the two processes can also be combined in one object.

Misregistration — analytical study term | Definition
Course reading: Misregistration is unintended misalignment between successive printed components, often visible where one colour shifts relative to another or to a key outline. This term is added from the corpus brief.

European Print and Indian Bazaar | Slide Context
### Module 6, slide 1

**Heading context:** Module 6: European Print and Indian Bazaar

Course reading: The Calcutta Art Studio Buddha and the Agra print introduce two uses of reproducible imagery: devotional circulation and a published architectural view. The Agra credits separate sketch, drawing and engraving. European print technology and South Asian subjects therefore require separate statements about medium, audience and labour.

**Same slide:** [Buddhadeb — Calcutta Art Studio](<buddhadeb-calcutta-art-studio.md>).

**Same heading group:** [Buddhadeb — Calcutta Art Studio](<buddhadeb-calcutta-art-studio.md>), [Fort at Agra — Bacon, Stanfield and Kernot](<fort-at-agra-bacon-stanfield-and-kernot.md>).

### Module 6, slide 3

**Heading context:** Indigenous Printing in the Indian subcontinent

Course reading: The unfinished Pedana woodblocks and finished Polavaram cotton connect a carved matrix to textile printing. This precedes the European Saint Sebastian block-and-impression pair. The sequence compares a printing principle across supports and uses, while keeping the specific practices distinct.

**Same slide:** [Kalamkari printed cotton — Polavaram](<kalamkari-printed-cotton-polavaram.md>), [Relief, intaglio and planography](<relief-intaglio-and-planography.md>), [Unfinished textile woodblocks — Pedana](<unfinished-textile-woodblocks-pedana.md>).

**Same heading group:** [Kalamkari printed cotton — Polavaram](<kalamkari-printed-cotton-polavaram.md>), [Relief, intaglio and planography](<relief-intaglio-and-planography.md>), [Unfinished textile woodblocks — Pedana](<unfinished-textile-woodblocks-pedana.md>).

**Heading context:** Types of Printmaking (continued from slide 4)

Course reading: The Sicri Gully and Salsette temple prints are followed by the Antiquities of India title page. Views, maker credits and antiquarian publication framing connect Indian sites with a British audience. Pictorial composition and the date of a published plate remain separate from the date of a visit or monument.

### Module 6, slide 9

**Heading context:** Print and Colonial Documentation of People, Places and Plants in the Indian Subcontinent

Course reading: Solvyns’s potters and bazaar, the Kanaree cave view and Roxburgh’s botanical plate form a sequence of people, places and plants under colonial documentation. Each image organizes knowledge differently. The grouping asks who observes, draws, commissions and publishes, as well as what is represented.

title: Portrait of Émile Zola

The screen includes a small bird on a flowering branch. A feather quill rises from an ornamental desk vessel. A blue booklet visibly bears Manet’s name. The wall grouping contains Olympia, a Japanese standing figure and a partly obscured monochrome group.

The Letter — Mary Cassatt | Distinctions
**Exam distractor:** “Cassatt’s The Letter is a woodblock directly derived from Mizuno’s later After the Bath.”

### Module 7, slide 13

**Heading context:** Photographic representation of Japan

Course reading: The photographic portraits of Monet and Cassatt are followed by Beato’s staged performers. These photographs connect the artists and Japan to specific modes of representation. Sitter identification, photographic authorship, staging and hand-colouring are separate questions rather than one transparent documentary fact.

**Same slide:** [Geisha’s Dancing — Beato studio attribution](<geishas-dancing-beato-studio-attribution.md>).

### Module 7, slide 14

**Heading context:** Photography and photographers in Japan

Course reading: The Tokyo street photograph and Yoshikazu’s print of French people using a camera reverse the direction of looking. Japan appears as an urban photographic subject while Europeans become the subject of a Japanese print. Orientalism/Occidentalism is therefore discussed through representation and agency, not simply the nationality of an image’s subject.

text:
Japonisme — appreciation, collecting and appropriation | Distinctions
**Exam distractor:** “Japonisme requires European artists to adopt Japanese woodblock manufacture rather than adapt pictorial devices.”

**Why it is wrong:** Van Gogh and Monet adapt Japanese pictorial resources in painting, while Cassatt uses intaglio. Japonisme concerns reception and transformation, including cases where the European artist retains a different medium.

title: Asia in Amsterdam — entrance and gallery arrangements
source: ART403 Module 8, slide 4; ART403 Module 8, slide 5 (visual analysis)
text:
Asia in Amsterdam — entrance and gallery arrangements | Physical Arrangement
At the entrance, large exhibition lettering fills a deep blue wall at right. Two decorated cylindrical objects occupy stepped blue niches along the route. An enlarged harbour scene covers the rear-left wall, with a floral hanging visible beyond it. In the smaller gallery view, a narrative tapestry spans the left wall, two tall glass cases stand on the floor, and framed pictures run along the right wall toward a doorway. In the long gallery, cabinets and textiles line the left, still-life paintings line the right, and central cases, paired tall vessels and a rear screen establish an axis under the skylight. The nearest right-hand still life visibly includes a blue-and-white ewer.

### Module 8, slide 9

**Heading context:** Understanding interconnections, mass production and social life of objects through maritime history

Course reading: Belitung bowls arranged as waves around a dhow are compared with underwater documentation and Kerkar’s encrusted cross. The museum uses repeated cargo to give production and shipping a spatial form; the underwater image records another stage of the objects’ lives. The cross introduces the ocean’s material participation in contemporary making.

text:
Animal motifs: identification before symbolism | Slide Context
**M2:1**

Course reading: The full palampore and its detail introduce Coromandel textiles through overall field organization and close motif comparison. The production map on slide 2 then connects this object-centred reading to named places and routes, while the later demonstrations reveal the makers’ processes.

**M2:6, M2:7**

Course reading: The five-panel tent and enlarged two-headed bird are compared with a Manga malai necklace and a Dutch-cemetery gravestone. The Gandaberunda form connects textile, jewellery and carved stone across different uses. The grouping demonstrates motif mobility; the ritual, military and commemorative functions must still be distinguished.

**M2:9**

Course reading: The Bijapur mihrab and Golconda gateway extend the textile discussion into architectural framing and ornament. Compare arched compartments, vegetal design and surface pattern with the preceding hangings. The next Dutch warehouse introduces the commercial infrastructure through which textiles and designs circulated.

**M2:13**

Course reading: The Golconda coverlet is paired with the hanging of Manikkavachar and Meenakshi’s wedding. Courtly imagery and religious narrative distinguish the two textiles even where borders and repeated figures invite formal comparison. The heading asks how to differentiate kalamkari works, not how to treat them as one subject.

**M3:9**

Course reading: Ibrahim Adil Shah on Atash Khan is paired with enthroned Sarasvati under cultural amalgamation. Courtly self-presentation and a deity of learning and music share the discussion. The next Kitab-e-Nauras page and Sangeet Mahal translate this relationship into text, patronage and a musical setting.

**M3:18**

Course reading: The zoomorphic dagger hilt is followed by Sultan Ali Adil Shah I under a question about their relationship. A portable court object and a ruler’s portrait link animal ornament, costume and elite identity. The juxtaposition asks how object culture and represented kingship illuminate one another.

**M3:23**

Course reading: The Golconda Adoration of the Christ Child and Badshahi Ashurkhana interior share the heading Amalgamation of Persianate and European Themes. Painting and ritual architecture demonstrate different forms of religious and visual practice in the same regional discussion. They are complementary examples, not evidence that both serve one ritual.

**M3:24**

Course reading: Collaert’s bird engraving, the parrot-and-ram painting and the dervish gathering place animal imagery and human settings side by side. The sequence asks how motifs and ways of seeing move between European print and Deccani painting.

title: Animal motifs: identification before symbolism
source: ART403 Module 2, slide 1; ART403 Module 2, slide 6; ART403 Module 2, slide 7; ART403 Module 2, slide 9; ART403 Module 2, slide 13; ART403 Module 3, slide 9; ART403 Module 3, slide 18; ART403 Module 3, slide 23; ART403 Module 3, slide 24; ART403 Module 4, slide 9; ART403 Module 4, slide 10; ART403 Module 5, slide 2; ART403 Module 5, slide 5; ART403 Module 5, slide 6; ART403 Module 5, slide 13; ART403 Module 5, slide 16; ART403 Module 6, slide 13 + https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/figural-representation-in-islamic-art
text:
Animal motifs: identification before symbolism | Slide Context
 A related bird or animal does not erase differences of subject, composition and use.

**M4:9, M4:10**

Course reading: Peacocks in a garden and dead partridges in a still life compare living display with arranged game. The trade-goods and exotic discussion asks how birds enter collections, consumption and images. Their shared animal subject does not make the scenes interchangeable or give them one fixed symbolic code.

**M5:2**

Course reading: The Mughal and Iranian animal carpets are placed within the question of continental and maritime trade. Their shared textile format supports comparison of animal imagery and production contexts across regions. The next muslin examples extend the enquiry from patterned furnishing to the material qualities of cloth.

**M5:5, M5:6**

Course reading: Basawan’s Virgin and Child is paired across adjacent slides with a work after Luini. The shared mother-and-child subject supports comparison of gesture, setting and modelling across Mughal and European images. The later date of the displayed Luini copy prevents treating that particular object as Basawan’s direct model.

**M5:13**

Course reading: The two Camel Fight images by or associated with Bihzad and Abd al-Samad are paired under Lineage or Silsila. A recurring subject and composition make transmission and emulation visible. The succeeding European-source studies extend this enquiry beyond one Persianate line of artistic association.

**M5:16**

Course reading: The queried Dürer Crucifixion, Abu’l Hasan’s Saint John and Abdullah Khan’s hawking scene place European print study alongside Mughal portraiture and courtly activity. These examples belong to the lineage discussion while differing in subject and making process. A European religious figure supplies a visual resource, not the identity of every local patron.

**M6:13**

Course reading: The broom scene and cat-with-lobster Kalighat painting are followed by the cat motif in a Battala print. Social commentary and a recognizable subject pass between painting and print. The repeated cat is therefore a comparison of pictorial treatment and circulation, not evidence that the two objects share one manufacturing process.

The Mangalore tile heading brings mission-industry history into the contemporary installation.

**M8:19**

Course reading: The framed elephant image is placed in relation to Quintessential’s screen, sculptural objects and fragmented forms. Under the Elephanta and colonial-legacy heading, archival representation and contemporary installation rework historical authority. Precise spatial relationships supply the curatorial argument, not the mere fact that several objects share a room.

They are complementary examples, not evidence that both serve one ritual.

Course reading: The Christian-imagery canteen and Birth of the Prophet Muhammad are grouped under a discussion of early modern empires and Christianity. Their different media and earlier dates widen the history of Abrahamic imagery beyond one Mughal moment. A thematic heading is not the manufacture date of either object.

**M6:17**

Course reading: The lithographed book cover, tiger-shaped script and hawk-shaped script compare writing as readable content and constructed image. Lithography and colour lithography provide different printed realizations. The grouping connects text, animal outline and circulation rather than treating the animal forms as natural-history studies.

text:
Maps and globes: knowledge, representation and power | Slide Context
**M2:2**

Course reading: The Coromandel map, route diagram and riverside temple landscape connect textile production to places, movement and built environments. This sequence leads from the opening palampore to named making practices. A historical map and a modern route diagram contribute different kinds of geographical evidence.

**M3:15**

Course reading: The rounded Bijapur plan follows the discussion of travelling techniques and precedes Gol Gumbaz. The heading asks about Kakatiya connections, using urban shape as a historical question. The next tomb supplies a specific building within the city rather than proof of that proposed planning genealogy.

**M3:21**

Course reading: The Hyderabad map and street view toward Charminar pair planned urban order with a view through monumental space. Under City of Gardens, the lecture applies chahar-bagh ordering at city scale. The older Lotus Mahal comparison supplies another architectural connection, while the map has its own later date.

**M4:2**

Course reading: Vosmaer’s flowers and Vermeer’s Geographer place an oceanic argument within a vase, textile, map and globe. The still life and inhabited interior connect collected goods with geographical knowledge and pictorial skill. The subsequent VOC material makes the commercial network explicit.

**M5:1**

Course reading: The Mughal and Iranian animal carpets are placed within the question of continental and maritime trade. Their shared textile format supports comparison of animal imagery and production contexts across regions. The next muslin examples extend the enquiry from patterned furnishing to the material qualities of cloth.

**M5:4**

Course reading: Akbar and Adham Khan is used to discuss sartorial choices and a ruler’s legitimacy after the muslin sequence. Clothing operates as a political visual language, not simply surface pattern. The following Christian-subject paintings extend the enquiry into the Mughal court’s selective use of different visual resources.

**M5:5**

Course reading: Basawan’s Virgin and Child is paired across adjacent slides with a work after Luini. The shared mother-and-child subject supports comparison of gesture, setting and modelling across Mughal and European images. The later date of the displayed Luini copy prevents treating that particular object as Basawan’s direct model.

**M5:7**

Course reading: Akbar’s combat-of-ascetics scene and Leonardo’s Virgin of the Rocks place Mughal atelier practice beside European Renaissance composition. Crowded action and the contained devotional grouping provide different organizations of figures and space. The sequence broadens artistic encounter beyond a claim of simple copying.

**M5:10**

title: Maps and globes: knowledge, representation and power
source: ART403 Module 2, slide 2; ART403 Module 3, slide 15; ART403 Module 3, slide 21; ART403 Module 4, slide 2; ART403 Module 5, slide 1; ART403 Module 5, slide 4; ART403 Module 5, slide 5; ART403 Module 5, slide 7; ART403 Module 5, slide 10; ART403 Module 5, slide 12; ART403 Module 5, slide 18; ART403 Module 5, slide 19; ART403 Module 5, slide 20; ART403 Module 5, slide 21; ART403 Module 5, slide 23 + https://journals.gmu.edu/whc/article/download/4117/2316
text:
Maps and globes: knowledge, representation and power | Slide Context
Course reading: The Mughal Deposition follows the church and European painting sequence under Derivative? Altered? Creative? The familiar Christian subject becomes a test of adaptation in figures, setting and handling. Slide 17 returns to it beside Raimondi’s print so that a broad encounter can be examined as a particular composition comparison.

**M5:12**

Course reading: Ghulam’s Virgin and Child sits within the discussion of collecting and studying classical texts from diverse traditions at the Mughal court. The image becomes a case of active selection and translation between pictorial worlds. The following Bihzad–Abd al-Samad comparison makes artistic lineage a more specific mechanism.

**M5:18**

Course reading: The Gulshan sheet assembles a Luna engraving with Persian drawings of a seated man, a group of men and a lion. The whole and its components must be read together: collecting, cutting, mounting and framing create a new relationship among previously separate images. One page therefore need not have one maker, date or original medium.

**M5:19, M5:20**

Course reading: The full Jahangir–Malik Ambar allegory and its details connect the emperor’s body to a mapped globe, cosmic supports and a defeated enemy. The India-centred globe is part of a political claim. Repeated enlargement trains attention to the small devices through which cartographic form becomes imperial imagery.

**M5:21**

Course reading: Jahangir’s embrace of Shah Abbas uses a mapped globe and unequal figure scale for an allegory of sovereignty; the next folio places Jahangir with Jesus in separate images. The sequence compares the court’s political and religious visual resources. An embrace or shared page does not establish equal power or a single religious identity.

**M5:23**

Course reading: Shah Jahan’s halo, angels and portrait pendant are followed by a comparison with the standing-ruler drawing associated in the lecture with Rembrandt. The sequence tracks courtly self-representation and its reception across media. Maker, represented ruler and later interpreter perform different roles in that connection.

text:
Christian imagery in South Asian and Persianate settings | Slide Context
**M3:23**

Course reading: The Golconda Adoration of the Christ Child and Badshahi Ashurkhana interior share the heading Amalgamation of Persianate and European Themes. Painting and ritual architecture demonstrate different forms of religious and visual practice in the same regional discussion. They are complementary examples, not evidence that both serve one ritual.

**M5:5, M5:6**

Course reading: Basawan’s Virgin and Child is paired across adjacent slides with a work after Luini. The shared mother-and-child subject supports comparison of gesture, setting and modelling across Mughal and European images. The later date of the displayed Luini copy prevents treating that particular object as Basawan’s direct model.

**M5:8**

Course reading: Akbar’s combat-of-ascetics scene and Leonardo’s Virgin of the Rocks place Mughal atelier practice beside European Renaissance composition. Crowded action and the contained devotional grouping provide different organizations of figures and space. The sequence broadens artistic encounter beyond a claim of simple copying.

**M5:9**

Course reading: Akbar’s Church is placed between Renaissance imagery and the Mughal Deposition. The building supplies a setting for the module’s discussion of religious communities and encounters. It links architecture to the circulation of Christian subjects without assigning every surviving architectural part to one original phase.

**M5:10**

Course reading: The Mughal Deposition follows the church and European painting sequence under Derivative? Altered? Creative? The familiar Christian subject becomes a test of adaptation in figures, setting and handling. Slide 17 returns to it beside Raimondi’s print so that a broad encounter can be examined as a particular composition comparison.

**M5:11**

Course reading: The Christian-imagery canteen and Birth of the Prophet Muhammad are grouped under a discussion of early modern empires and Christianity. Their different media and earlier dates widen the history of Abrahamic imagery beyond one Mughal moment. A thematic heading is not the manufacture date of either object.

**M5:12**

Course reading: Ghulam’s Virgin and Child sits within the discussion of collecting and studying classical texts from diverse traditions at the Mughal court. The image becomes a case of active selection and translation between pictorial worlds. The following Bihzad–Abd al-Samad comparison makes artistic lineage a more specific mechanism.

**M5:15**

Course reading: The queried Dürer Crucifixion, Abu’l Hasan’s Saint John and Abdullah Khan’s hawking scene place European print study alongside Mughal portraiture and courtly activity.

title: Christian imagery in South Asian and Persianate settings
source: ART403 Module 3, slide 23; ART403 Module 5, slide 5; ART403 Module 5, slide 6; ART403 Module 5, slide 8; ART403 Module 5, slide 9; ART403 Module 5, slide 10; ART403 Module 5, slide 11; ART403 Module 5, slide 12; ART403 Module 5, slide 15; ART403 Module 5, slide 17; ART403 Module 5, slide 22; ART403 Module 8, slide 9; ART403 Module 8, slide 14; ART403 Module 8, slide 15 + https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/the-art-of-the-mughals-before-1600; https://www.nature.com/articles/s40494-021-00577-2
text:
Christian imagery in South Asian and Persianate settings | Slide Context
 These examples belong to the lineage discussion while differing in subject and making process. A European religious figure supplies a visual resource, not the identity of every local patron.

**M5:17**

Course reading: The Mughal Deposition is placed beside Raimondi’s Descent from the Cross after Raphael. Their shared narrative and related figure organization support a derivative/adaptive comparison. The paired view makes alteration and new handling part of the answer, rather than equating adaptation with mechanical reproduction.

**M5:22**

Course reading: Jahangir’s embrace of Shah Abbas uses a mapped globe and unequal figure scale for an allegory of sovereignty; the next folio places Jahangir with Jesus in separate images. The sequence compares the court’s political and religious visual resources. An embrace or shared page does not establish equal power or a single religious identity.

**M8:9**

Course reading: Belitung bowls arranged as waves around a dhow are compared with underwater documentation and Kerkar’s encrusted cross. The museum uses repeated cargo to give production and shipping a spatial form; the underwater image records another stage of the objects’ lives. The cross introduces the ocean’s material participation in contemporary making.

**M8:14, M8:15**

Course reading: Kerkar’s cross and the Museum of Goa title card develop the question of collaborating with the ocean. Encrustation, the cross form and its documentation connect material change to a recognizable cultural sign. This moves beyond the Belitung display’s reconstruction of past shipping into present artistic agency.

source: ART403 Module 6, slide 1; ART403 Module 6, slide 17; ART403 Module 6, slide 18; ART403 Module 6, slide 19; ART403 Module 6, slide 20 + https://sas-space.sas.ac.uk/10200/7/Tools%2C%20Machines%2C%20and%20Techniques%20for%20Printing%20Colour%20in%2018th-Century%20Europe%2C%20in%20Printing%20Colour%201700%E2%80%931830%2C%20pp%2021%E2%80%9351.pdf; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/786756
text:
Chromolithography: colour lithographic printing | Slide Context
**M6:1**

Course reading: The Calcutta Art Studio Buddha and the Agra print introduce two uses of reproducible imagery: devotional circulation and a published architectural view. The Agra credits separate sketch, drawing and engraving. European print technology and South Asian subjects therefore require separate statements about medium, audience and labour.

**M6:17**

Course reading: The lithographed book cover, tiger-shaped script and hawk-shaped script compare writing as readable content and constructed image. Lithography and colour lithography provide different printed realizations. The grouping connects text, animal outline and circulation rather than treating the animal forms as natural-history studies.

**M6:18**

Course reading: The Bombay scene and Annoda Prosad Bagchi’s Vijaya pair different makers and subjects within the print economy. They follow the book and calligraphic prints and precede studio devotional sheets. The comparison expands the field of print production beyond a single colonial publisher or one religious audience.

**M6:19, M6:20**

Course reading: Kali/Tara, the Calcutta Art Studio Buddha and the Pune Mahavir print form a sequence of studio devotional images. Different religious subjects use reproducible colour imagery and commercial publication. The significant distinction is between the regional subject, the technology and the agency of the producing studio.

title: Collecting and the changing life of objects
source: ART403 Module 7, slide 5; ART403 Module 7, slide 7; ART403 Module 8, slide 20 + https://bulletin.rijksmuseum.nl/article/download/9834/10330/16231
text:
Collecting and the changing life of objects | Definition and Grounded Significance
Course reading: Collections assemble objects into new relationships. The Asia in Amsterdam exhibition connected imported goods and images of consumption, while the lecture’s albums and textile displays show other acts of selection. Production, acquisition, mounting and exhibition need separate records.

title: Collecting and the changing life of objects
source: ART403 Module 7, slide 5; ART403 Module 7, slide 7; ART403 Module 8, slide 20 + https://bulletin.rijksmuseum.nl/article/download/9834/10330/16231
text:
Collecting and the changing life of objects | Slide Context
**M7:5**

Course reading: Père Tanguy’s Japanese-print backdrop is followed by Sunflowers and Almond Blossoms under Van Gogh’s imagined Japan. Collecting, colour, contour and cropped plant forms offer different ways to engage Japanese imagery. Japanese influence is therefore broader than a Japanese subject or the direct copy of one print.

**M7:7**

Course reading: Zola’s portrait and the enlarged reproductions on its wall make artistic association visible inside an interior. Olympia, a Japanese figure and a monochrome group are objects of pictorial reference within Manet’s painting. The components connect collecting to portrait identity without becoming separately inspected original prints.

**M8:20**

Course reading: The Vijaya Vitthala warrior, Ascetic Riding a Nag and Père Tanguy form the final recap. Stone carving, a marbled painting and a European portrait surrounded by Japanese prints supply three different histories of connection. Reclaiming oceanic ties means attending to those mechanisms of encounter and agency rather than treating regions as visually isolated.

text:
Colonial documentation and selective visibility | Slide Context
**M6:1, M6:2**

Course reading: The Calcutta Art Studio Buddha and the Agra print introduce two uses of reproducible imagery: devotional circulation and a published architectural view. The Agra credits separate sketch, drawing and engraving. European print technology and South Asian subjects therefore require separate statements about medium, audience and labour.

**M6:3**

Course reading: The unfinished Pedana woodblocks and finished Polavaram cotton connect a carved matrix to textile printing. This precedes the European Saint Sebastian block-and-impression pair. The sequence compares a printing principle across supports and uses, while keeping the specific practices distinct.

**M6:7, M6:8**

Course reading: The Sicri Gully and Salsette temple prints are followed by the Antiquities of India title page. Views, maker credits and antiquarian publication framing connect Indian sites with a British audience. Pictorial composition and the date of a published plate remain separate from the date of a visit or monument.

**M6:9, M6:10, M6:11, M6:12**

Course reading: Solvyns’s potters and bazaar, the Kanaree cave view and Roxburgh’s botanical plate form a sequence of people, places and plants under colonial documentation. Each image organizes knowledge differently. The grouping asks who observes, draws, commissions and publishes, as well as what is represented.

**M6:13, M6:14**

Course reading: The broom scene and cat-with-lobster Kalighat painting are followed by the cat motif in a Battala print. Social commentary and a recognizable subject pass between painting and print. The repeated cat is therefore a comparison of pictorial treatment and circulation, not evidence that the two objects share one manufacturing process.

**M6:17**

Course reading: The lithographed book cover, tiger-shaped script and hawk-shaped script compare writing as readable content and constructed image. Lithography and colour lithography provide different printed realizations. The grouping connects text, animal outline and circulation rather than treating the animal forms as natural-history studies.

**M6:18**

Course reading: The Bombay scene and Annoda Prosad Bagchi’s Vijaya pair different makers and subjects within the print economy. They follow the book and calligraphic prints and precede studio devotional sheets. The comparison expands the field of print production beyond a single colonial publisher or one religious audience.

**M6:19, M6:20, M6:21**

Under the Elephanta and colonial-legacy heading, archival representation and contemporary installation rework historical authority. Precise spatial relationships supply the curatorial argument, not the mere fact that several objects share a room.

text:
Conceptual authorship and execution | Definition and Grounded Significance
Course reading: LeWitt’s account separates an artwork’s prior conception from its execution. This supplies a framework for examining how an idea, fabrication and presentation can involve different roles. It does not erase craft labour or establish who conceived an anonymous work in a slide.

title: Conceptual authorship and execution
source: ART403 Module 8, slide 9; ART403 Module 8, slide 14; ART403 Module 8, slide 15; ART403 Module 8, slide 18 + https://www.moma.org/documents/moma_catalogue_1971_300297572.pdf

Conceptual authorship and execution | Slide Context
**M8:9**

Course reading: Belitung bowls arranged as waves around a dhow are compared with underwater documentation and Kerkar’s encrusted cross. The museum uses repeated cargo to give production and shipping a spatial form; the underwater image records another stage of the objects’ lives. The cross introduces the ocean’s material participation in contemporary making.

**M8:14, M8:15**

Course reading: Kerkar’s cross and the Museum of Goa title card develop the question of collaborating with the ocean. Encrustation, the cross form and its documentation connect material change to a recognizable cultural sign. This moves beyond the Belitung display’s reconstruction of past shipping into present artistic agency.

**M8:18**

Course reading: Tallur’s seated figure with a log is paired with Veni, vidi, vici’s passage between banks of roof tiles. Bodily encounter and material transformation connect the works, while their arrangements remain distinct. The Mangalore tile heading brings mission-industry history into the contemporary installation.

Connected histories as the course method | Definition and Grounded Significance
Course reading: The course reads art through movement among places, communities and media. Textile trade, Persianate court culture and imported print adaptation supply documented examples. The methodological claim is to examine evidenced relationships while retaining different regional histories. It is not a claim that all similarities share one cause.

text:
Connected histories as the course method | Slide Context
**M1:1, M1:2, M1:3, M1:4**

Course reading: The cover pairs a floral ceramic dish and floral fabric with a stone trader-and-horses relief under Ebb and Flow: Art and Globalism of Oceanic Networks. Repeated flowers connect ceramic and textile; the relief contributes the people and traded animals. This cross-media grouping argues for the circulation of goods, designs and artisanal knowledge through contact. The Paigah Tombs and Coromandel kalamkari hanging on slides 2–3 extend that argument into architectural ornament, textile making and human interaction.

**M1:5, M1:6**

Course reading: The empire and city maps establish several scales for reading the Mahanabami Dibba: territorial power, the Hampi landscape and individual monuments. The following temple hall and sculpture comparison turn this geographical frame into an investigation of structure, carving and historical difference.

**M2:2**

Course reading: The Coromandel map, route diagram and riverside temple landscape connect textile production to places, movement and built environments. This sequence leads from the opening palampore to named making practices. A historical map and a modern route diagram contribute different kinds of geographical evidence.

**M2:10**

Course reading: The Dutch warehouse follows the textile–architecture comparison and precedes the detailed reading of the Golconda coverlet. It places patterned goods and their imagery within trade infrastructure. The course asks how markets and contact participate in making visuals, as well as moving finished objects.

**M2:15**

Course reading: The Coromandel dodot moves the discussion from motif comparison to use in Southeast Asia. Its pairing in the sequence with European chintz garments on slide 16 shows a production region serving different dress forms and markets. Manufacture and destination are separate roles in the argument.

**M2:16**

Course reading: The chintz jacket and petticoat form a coordinated European dress ensemble. Following the Javanese dodot, they show Indian cotton entering distinct overseas clothing practices. Shared textile circulation therefore produces different social uses and silhouettes, rather than one uniform export style.

**M3:1, M3:2**

Course reading: The Persianate World / Persian Cosmopolis discussion uses Siesta to connect a Deccani scene with a wider courtly visual culture. The following madrasa comparison extends the enquiry from painting to architecture. Persianate connection is a framework for local adaptation, not a statement that every work was made in Iran.

**M3:4**

text:
Connected histories as the course method | Slide Context
Course reading: Mahmud Gawan Madrasa is compared with Ulugh Beg’s madrasa and the Registan under Timurid Central Asian culture in Deccan. Monumental entrances, towers and patterned surfaces supply the architectural comparison. The next Bidar landscape slide broadens the enquiry to water, gardens and the siting of buildings.

**M3:6**

Course reading: The Bidri sailabchi and Iranian ghalamzani vessel compare decorative metalworking across Deccan and Iran. Contrasting inlay on a dark ground and worked surface detail direct attention to different processes. This object-making slide extends the architectural comparison into portable craft.

**M3:8**

Course reading: The turbaned miniature detail introduces close attention to painted faces and clothing; the next slide locates Farrukh Beg within a travelling artist’s career and album culture. Stylistic observation and a named biography contribute different evidence to the discussion of moving artists.

**M5:1**

Course reading: The Mughal and Iranian animal carpets are placed within the question of continental and maritime trade. Their shared textile format supports comparison of animal imagery and production contexts across regions. The next muslin examples extend the enquiry from patterned furnishing to the material qualities of cloth.

**M5:4**

Course reading: Akbar and Adham Khan is used to discuss sartorial choices and a ruler’s legitimacy after the muslin sequence. Clothing operates as a political visual language, not simply surface pattern. The following Christian-subject paintings extend the enquiry into the Mughal court’s selective use of different visual resources.

**M5:5**

Course reading: Basawan’s Virgin and Child is paired across adjacent slides with a work after Luini. The shared mother-and-child subject supports comparison of gesture, setting and modelling across Mughal and European images. The later date of the displayed Luini copy prevents treating that particular object as Basawan’s direct model.

**M5:7**

Course reading: Akbar’s combat-of-ascetics scene and Leonardo’s Virgin of the Rocks place Mughal atelier practice beside European Renaissance composition. Crowded action and the contained devotional grouping provide different organizations of figures and space. The sequence broadens artistic encounter beyond a claim of simple copying.

**M5:10**

Course reading: The Mughal Deposition follows the church and European painting sequence under Derivative? Altered? Creative? The familiar Christian subject becomes a test of adaptation in figures, setting and handling. Slide 17 returns to it beside Raimondi’s print so that a broad encounter can be examined as a particular composition comparison.

**M5:12**

text:
Connected histories as the course method | Slide Context
Course reading: Ghulam’s Virgin and Child sits within the discussion of collecting and studying classical texts from diverse traditions at the Mughal court. The image becomes a case of active selection and translation between pictorial worlds. The following Bihzad–Abd al-Samad comparison makes artistic lineage a more specific mechanism.

**M5:18**

Course reading: The Gulshan sheet assembles a Luna engraving with Persian drawings of a seated man, a group of men and a lion. The whole and its components must be read together: collecting, cutting, mounting and framing create a new relationship among previously separate images. One page therefore need not have one maker, date or original medium.

**M5:19, M5:20**

Course reading: The full Jahangir–Malik Ambar allegory and its details connect the emperor’s body to a mapped globe, cosmic supports and a defeated enemy. The India-centred globe is part of a political claim. Repeated enlargement trains attention to the small devices through which cartographic form becomes imperial imagery.

**M5:21**

Course reading: Jahangir’s embrace of Shah Abbas uses a mapped globe and unequal figure scale for an allegory of sovereignty; the next folio places Jahangir with Jesus in separate images. The sequence compares the court’s political and religious visual resources. An embrace or shared page does not establish equal power or a single religious identity.

**M5:23**

Course reading: Shah Jahan’s halo, angels and portrait pendant are followed by a comparison with the standing-ruler drawing associated in the lecture with Rembrandt. The sequence tracks courtly self-representation and its reception across media. Maker, represented ruler and later interpreter perform different roles in that connection.

**M8:1, M8:2**

Course reading: The Ahmedabad exhibition poster frames its title with a floral trade-textile detail. The original cloth becomes the visual identity of a contemporary exhibition about distant markets. The ensuing museum sequence examines how present displays assemble evidence for those historical connections.

**M8:3**

Course reading: The Interwoven Globe entrance banner and gallery sightline connect an exhibition’s public framing with its arrangement of textiles and images. Position, scale and the view through the gallery invite cross-object comparisons. The next Asia in Amsterdam installation provides a second curatorial method for presenting historical circulation.

**M8:4**

Course reading: Asia in Amsterdam places imported Asian goods near paintings that represent luxury consumption, with vessels and furniture in cases and textiles or pictures on walls. The entrance image and successive gallery views make trade visible through juxtaposition. A painting of a vessel and an exhibited vessel have complementary evidential roles.

text:
Connected histories as the course method | Slide Context
**M8:7**

Course reading: The Mumbai trade-textile graphic, ROM display and Southeast Asian Ramayana textile connect contemporary curatorial framing with different uses of Indian cloth. Their sequence distinguishes an exhibition identity, an arranged group of garments and an individual ceremonial textile. Market, subject and present display are different parts of its social history.

**M8:9, M8:10**

Course reading: Belitung bowls arranged as waves around a dhow are compared with underwater documentation and Kerkar’s encrusted cross. The museum uses repeated cargo to give production and shipping a spatial form; the underwater image records another stage of the objects’ lives. The cross introduces the ocean’s material participation in contemporary making.

**M8:14**

Course reading: Kerkar’s cross and the Museum of Goa title card develop the question of collaborating with the ocean. Encrustation, the cross form and its documentation connect material change to a recognizable cultural sign. This moves beyond the Belitung display’s reconstruction of past shipping into present artistic agency.

**M8:16**

Course reading: The Fort Kochi opening poster and two It’s my Biennale portrait designs put an international exhibition into ordinary local streets. Repetition and the first-person slogan connect public ownership with place. The following installations show how the event’s regional identity is developed through particular works and historical connections.

**M8:17**

Course reading: Raghavan’s container-ship work connects the Biblical Tarshish reference with contemporary shipping under Biblical Ties and Trade. It follows the street campaign and precedes Tallur’s tile installation. The sequence makes historical narrative, current commerce and local material history different ways of reclaiming global ties.

**M8:18**

Course reading: Tallur’s seated figure with a log is paired with Veni, vidi, vici’s passage between banks of roof tiles. Bodily encounter and material transformation connect the works, while their arrangements remain distinct. The Mangalore tile heading brings mission-industry history into the contemporary installation.

**M8:19**

Course reading: The framed elephant image is placed in relation to Quintessential’s screen, sculptural objects and fragmented forms. Under the Elephanta and colonial-legacy heading, archival representation and contemporary installation rework historical authority. Precise spatial relationships supply the curatorial argument, not the mere fact that several objects share a room.

**M8:20**

Course reading: The Vijaya Vitthala warrior, Ascetic Riding a Nag and Père Tanguy form the final recap. Stone carving, a marbled painting and a European portrait surrounded by Japanese prints supply three different histories of connection.

Costume as evidence, with limits | Slide Context
**M5:4**

Course reading: Akbar and Adham Khan is used to discuss sartorial choices and a ruler’s legitimacy after the muslin sequence. Clothing operates as a political visual language, not simply surface pattern. The following Christian-subject paintings extend the enquiry into the Mughal court’s selective use of different visual resources.

**M7:10**

Course reading: La Japonaise, Cassatt’s The Letter and Mizuno’s After the Bath compare costume performance, domestic pictorial design and a Japanese print. The three illustrate different forms of Japanese reception. Cassatt’s intaglio medium remains distinct from woodblock, and Mizuno’s later print cannot be her direct source.

The course’s social dimension asks whose labour becomes visible and whose name is retained in conventional attribution.

text:
Craft agency and the distribution of credit | Slide Context
**M1:1**

Course reading: The cover pairs a floral ceramic dish and floral fabric with a stone trader-and-horses relief under Ebb and Flow: Art and Globalism of Oceanic Networks. Repeated flowers connect ceramic and textile; the relief contributes the people and traded animals. This cross-media grouping argues for the circulation of goods, designs and artisanal knowledge through contact. The Paigah Tombs and Coromandel kalamkari hanging on slides 2–3 extend that argument into architectural ornament, textile making and human interaction.

**M1:16**

Course reading: The trader with horses is placed beside a wootz dagger under Trade connections, with textiles named in the lecture discussion. The grouping connects traded animals, metal and cloth to royal imagery. The collar and performer comparisons on slides 17–18 extend commerce into the movement of dress and visual forms.

**M1:25**

Course reading: The royal platform, horse trader, hero stone and warrior recap the module’s cultural/trade argument. Ceremony, commerce, commemoration and martial imagery contribute different evidence. Their grouping joins social and political functions to travelling forms; it does not reduce Hampi’s art to one exclusively religious or decorative meaning.

**M2:4, M2:5**

Course reading: The Srikalahasti drawing demonstration and Polavaram block-printing demonstration are paired across adjacent slides, with a finished Coromandel hanging beside the latter. They separate making with a pen, repeating with a block and the resulting coloured cloth. The comparison gives craft labour a place alongside design and trade.

**M3:8**

Course reading: The turbaned miniature detail introduces close attention to painted faces and clothing; the next slide locates Farrukh Beg within a travelling artist’s career and album culture. Stylistic observation and a named biography contribute different evidence to the discussion of moving artists.

**M3:13**

Course reading: The marbling demonstration is placed with Ascetic Riding a Nag, followed by another thin rider on a marbled horse. Process and finished imagery explain how abri patterns become part of a figure-ground composition. The technique comparison is firmer than assigning one exclusive spiritual or literary identity to each rider.

**M3:25**

Course reading: Farrukh Beg’s presumed self-portrait, Ascetic Riding a Nag and Sultan Ali Adil Shah I recap the module through travelling artists, marbled technique and courtly identity. Each supplies a different mechanism of connection. Their grouping makes movement of people, processes and imagery jointly significant.

**M4:1, M4:2, M4:3**

text:
Craft agency and the distribution of credit | Slide Context
Course reading: Vosmaer’s flowers and Vermeer’s Geographer place an oceanic argument within a vase, textile, map and globe. The still life and inhabited interior connect collected goods with geographical knowledge and pictorial skill. The subsequent VOC material makes the commercial network explicit.

**M4:4, M4:5**

Course reading: The VOC ship model and lavish lobster-and-fruit still life connect transport with the consumption and display of goods. Between Amsterdam and Asia develops into a discussion of materiality and trade. The painted table is therefore read through economic circulation as well as arrangement, colour and texture.

**M4:6**

Course reading: The goldsmith’s balance, goods, customers and convex mirror follow the discussion of traded possessions. The shop makes exchange and skilled work visible within a densely organized interior. The next timepiece still life extends attention to crafted objects, time and the values attached to possession.

**M4:7, M4:8**

Course reading: The timepiece and armour still lifes group crafted objects with carefully rendered surfaces. Under the time devoted to making objects discussion, they connect labour and visual attention to possession, transience or status. Different selected objects support different meanings within the still-life format.

**M4:9, M4:10**

Course reading: Peacocks in a garden and dead partridges in a still life compare living display with arranged game. The trade-goods and exotic discussion asks how birds enter collections, consumption and images. Their shared animal subject does not make the scenes interchangeable or give them one fixed symbolic code.

**M5:3**

Course reading: The revived Dhaka muslin sari and transparency demonstration compare a worn textile with a close presentation of its fineness. Under Prized Trade Goods, cloth’s material quality becomes part of its value and circulation. The next Akbar image links such attention to clothing with political self-presentation.

**M5:14**

Course reading: The two Camel Fight images by or associated with Bihzad and Abd al-Samad are paired under Lineage or Silsila. A recurring subject and composition make transmission and emulation visible. The succeeding European-source studies extend this enquiry beyond one Persianate line of artistic association.

**M6:1**

Course reading: The Calcutta Art Studio Buddha and the Agra print introduce two uses of reproducible imagery: devotional circulation and a published architectural view. The Agra credits separate sketch, drawing and engraving. European print technology and South Asian subjects therefore require separate statements about medium, audience and labour.

**M6:3**

text:
Craft agency and the distribution of credit | Slide Context
Course reading: The unfinished Pedana woodblocks and finished Polavaram cotton connect a carved matrix to textile printing. This precedes the European Saint Sebastian block-and-impression pair. The sequence compares a printing principle across supports and uses, while keeping the specific practices distinct.

**M6:7**

Course reading: The Sicri Gully and Salsette temple prints are followed by the Antiquities of India title page. Views, maker credits and antiquarian publication framing connect Indian sites with a British audience. Pictorial composition and the date of a published plate remain separate from the date of a visit or monument.

**M6:9, M6:12**

Course reading: Solvyns’s potters and bazaar, the Kanaree cave view and Roxburgh’s botanical plate form a sequence of people, places and plants under colonial documentation. Each image organizes knowledge differently. The grouping asks who observes, draws, commissions and publishes, as well as what is represented.

**M6:13, M6:14**

Course reading: The broom scene and cat-with-lobster Kalighat painting are followed by the cat motif in a Battala print. Social commentary and a recognizable subject pass between painting and print. The repeated cat is therefore a comparison of pictorial treatment and circulation, not evidence that the two objects share one manufacturing process.

**M6:17**

Course reading: The lithographed book cover, tiger-shaped script and hawk-shaped script compare writing as readable content and constructed image. Lithography and colour lithography provide different printed realizations. The grouping connects text, animal outline and circulation rather than treating the animal forms as natural-history studies.

**M6:18**

Course reading: The Bombay scene and Annoda Prosad Bagchi’s Vijaya pair different makers and subjects within the print economy. They follow the book and calligraphic prints and precede studio devotional sheets. The comparison expands the field of print production beyond a single colonial publisher or one religious audience.

**M6:19, M6:20, M6:21**

Course reading: Kali/Tara, the Calcutta Art Studio Buddha and the Pune Mahavir print form a sequence of studio devotional images. Different religious subjects use reproducible colour imagery and commercial publication. The significant distinction is between the regional subject, the technology and the agency of the producing studio.

**M8:7**

Course reading: The Mumbai trade-textile graphic, ROM display and Southeast Asian Ramayana textile connect contemporary curatorial framing with different uses of Indian cloth. Their sequence distinguishes an exhibition identity, an arranged group of garments and an individual ceremonial textile.

text:
Cusped and foliated arches | Definition and Grounded Significance
Course reading: A cusped arch has repeated lobes along its intrados or opening profile. The Hampi examples use such profiles within larger combinations of architectural forms. Identify the shape separately from the engineering: an ornamental arch can frame a load-bearing opening without itself revealing the complete construction.

text:
Cusped and foliated arches | Slide Context
**M1:2**

Course reading: The cover pairs a floral ceramic dish and floral fabric with a stone trader-and-horses relief under Ebb and Flow: Art and Globalism of Oceanic Networks. Repeated flowers connect ceramic and textile; the relief contributes the people and traded animals. This cross-media grouping argues for the circulation of goods, designs and artisanal knowledge through contact. The Paigah Tombs and Coromandel kalamkari hanging on slides 2–3 extend that argument into architectural ornament, textile making and human interaction.

**M1:23**

Course reading: The Lotus Mahal combines arches, posts, projecting eaves and tiered roof forms under an explicit heading about temple, palatial and Islamic architecture. The argument concerns the combination of structural and ornamental vocabularies within a courtly building. The next slide’s Charminar comparison follows those vocabularies across the Deccan.

**M1:24**

Course reading: Lotus Mahal and Charminar are brought together through stucco and cultural connections across the Deccan. Ornament supplies the bridge between distinct buildings and urban settings. This comparison develops the previous slide’s account of architectural combination rather than declaring the two monuments identical in structure or function.

**M2:5**

Course reading: The Srikalahasti drawing demonstration and Polavaram block-printing demonstration are paired across adjacent slides, with a finished Coromandel hanging beside the latter. They separate making with a pen, repeating with a block and the resulting coloured cloth. The comparison gives craft labour a place alongside design and trade.

**M2:6, M2:7**

Course reading: The five-panel tent and enlarged two-headed bird are compared with a Manga malai necklace and a Dutch-cemetery gravestone. The Gandaberunda form connects textile, jewellery and carved stone across different uses. The grouping demonstrates motif mobility; the ritual, military and commemorative functions must still be distinguished.

**M2:8**

Course reading: The Lepakshi procession mural and Golconda hanging compare figures, costume and ordered movement across wall painting and cloth. They follow the bird comparison across textile, jewellery and stone. The sequence makes visual translation between media part of the textile’s cultural history.

**M2:9**

Course reading: The Bijapur mihrab and Golconda gateway extend the textile discussion into architectural framing and ornament. Compare arched compartments, vegetal design and surface pattern with the preceding hangings. The next Dutch warehouse introduces the commercial infrastructure through which textiles and designs circulated.

text:

Course reading: In engraving, cut lines in a plate retain ink for transfer to paper. It is an intaglio process, distinct from raised-surface printing. A work can circulate through impressions while its design is adapted into another medium.

text:
Engraving and intaglio | Slide Context
**M3:24**

Course reading: Collaert’s bird engraving, the parrot-and-ram painting and the dervish gathering place animal imagery and human settings side by side. The sequence asks how motifs and ways of seeing move between European print and Deccani painting. A related bird or animal does not erase differences of subject, composition and use.

**M5:17**

Course reading: The Mughal Deposition is placed beside Raimondi’s Descent from the Cross after Raphael. Their shared narrative and related figure organization support a derivative/adaptive comparison. The paired view makes alteration and new handling part of the answer, rather than equating adaptation with mechanical reproduction.

**M6:2**

Course reading: The Calcutta Art Studio Buddha and the Agra print introduce two uses of reproducible imagery: devotional circulation and a published architectural view. The Agra credits separate sketch, drawing and engraving. European print technology and South Asian subjects therefore require separate statements about medium, audience and labour.

**M6:3**

Course reading: The unfinished Pedana woodblocks and finished Polavaram cotton connect a carved matrix to textile printing. This precedes the European Saint Sebastian block-and-impression pair. The sequence compares a printing principle across supports and uses, while keeping the specific practices distinct.

**M6:4**

Course reading: The Saint Sebastian woodblock and its impression are paired to make relief printing legible as a transfer process. Raised and cut-away areas relate to printed and unprinted areas. The following lithographic demonstration shows a different printing principle, so all reproducible images cannot be grouped as woodcuts.

**M6:5, M6:6**

Course reading: The lithographic stone demonstration and relief-printing video compare planographic and raised-surface printing. Matrix, inking and transfer provide the distinctions. The subsequent landscape prints show how reproducible processes serve published views, rather than making process and subject the same category.

**M6:7**

Course reading: The Sicri Gully and Salsette temple prints are followed by the Antiquities of India title page. Views, maker credits and antiquarian publication framing connect Indian sites with a British audience. Pictorial composition and the date of a published plate remain separate from the date of a visit or monument.

**M6:11**

Course reading: Solvyns’s potters and bazaar, the Kanaree cave view and Roxburgh’s botanical plate form a sequence of people, places and plants under colonial documentation. Each image organizes knowledge differently. The grouping asks who observes, draws, commissions and publishes, as well as what is represented.

source: ART403 Module 5, slide 1; ART403 Module 5, slide 4; ART403 Module 5, slide 5; ART403 Module 5, slide 6; ART403 Module 5, slide 7; ART403 Module 5, slide 10; ART403 Module 5, slide 12; ART403 Module 5, slide 15; ART403 Module 5, slide 17; ART403 Module 5, slide 18; ART403 Module 5, slide 19; ART403 Module 5, slide 20; ART403 Module 5, slide 21; ART403 Module 5, slide 23 + https://www.nature.com/articles/s40494-021-00577-2
text:
Firangi-sazi and European-derived pictorial devices | Slide Context
**M5:1**

Course reading: The Mughal and Iranian animal carpets are placed within the question of continental and maritime trade. Their shared textile format supports comparison of animal imagery and production contexts across regions. The next muslin examples extend the enquiry from patterned furnishing to the material qualities of cloth.

**M5:4**

Course reading: Akbar and Adham Khan is used to discuss sartorial choices and a ruler’s legitimacy after the muslin sequence. Clothing operates as a political visual language, not simply surface pattern. The following Christian-subject paintings extend the enquiry into the Mughal court’s selective use of different visual resources.

**M5:5, M5:6**

Course reading: Basawan’s Virgin and Child is paired across adjacent slides with a work after Luini. The shared mother-and-child subject supports comparison of gesture, setting and modelling across Mughal and European images. The later date of the displayed Luini copy prevents treating that particular object as Basawan’s direct model.

**M5:7**

Course reading: Akbar’s combat-of-ascetics scene and Leonardo’s Virgin of the Rocks place Mughal atelier practice beside European Renaissance composition. Crowded action and the contained devotional grouping provide different organizations of figures and space. The sequence broadens artistic encounter beyond a claim of simple copying.

**M5:10**

Course reading: The Mughal Deposition follows the church and European painting sequence under Derivative? Altered? Creative? The familiar Christian subject becomes a test of adaptation in figures, setting and handling. Slide 17 returns to it beside Raimondi’s print so that a broad encounter can be examined as a particular composition comparison.

**M5:12**

Course reading: Ghulam’s Virgin and Child sits within the discussion of collecting and studying classical texts from diverse traditions at the Mughal court. The image becomes a case of active selection and translation between pictorial worlds. The following Bihzad–Abd al-Samad comparison makes artistic lineage a more specific mechanism.

**M5:15**

Course reading: The queried Dürer Crucifixion, Abu’l Hasan’s Saint John and Abdullah Khan’s hawking scene place European print study alongside Mughal portraiture and courtly activity. These examples belong to the lineage discussion while differing in subject and making process. A European religious figure supplies a visual resource, not the identity of every local patron.

**M5:17**

Course reading: The Mughal Deposition is placed beside Raimondi’s Descent from the Cross after Raphael. Their shared narrative and related figure organization support a derivative/adaptive comparison.

Course reading: The Gulshan sheet assembles a Luna engraving with Persian drawings of a seated man, a group of men and a lion. The whole and its components must be read together: collecting, cutting, mounting and framing create a new relationship among previously separate images. One page therefore need not have one maker, date or original medium.

**M5:19, M5:20**

Course reading: The full Jahangir–Malik Ambar allegory and its details connect the emperor’s body to a mapped globe, cosmic supports and a defeated enemy. The India-centred globe is part of a political claim. Repeated enlargement trains attention to the small devices through which cartographic form becomes imperial imagery.

**M5:21**

Course reading: Jahangir’s embrace of Shah Abbas uses a mapped globe and unequal figure scale for an allegory of sovereignty; the next folio places Jahangir with Jesus in separate images. The sequence compares the court’s political and religious visual resources. An embrace or shared page does not establish equal power or a single religious identity.

**M5:23**

Course reading: Shah Jahan’s halo, angels and portrait pendant are followed by a comparison with the standing-ruler drawing associated in the lecture with Rembrandt. The sequence tracks courtly self-representation and its reception across media. Maker, represented ruler and later interpreter perform different roles in that connection.

text:
Flowers as travelling designs | Slide Context
**M1:1, M1:3**

Course reading: The cover pairs a floral ceramic dish and floral fabric with a stone trader-and-horses relief under Ebb and Flow: Art and Globalism of Oceanic Networks. Repeated flowers connect ceramic and textile; the relief contributes the people and traded animals. This cross-media grouping argues for the circulation of goods, designs and artisanal knowledge through contact. The Paigah Tombs and Coromandel kalamkari hanging on slides 2–3 extend that argument into architectural ornament, textile making and human interaction.

**M2:1**

Course reading: The full palampore and its detail introduce Coromandel textiles through overall field organization and close motif comparison. The production map on slide 2 then connects this object-centred reading to named places and routes, while the later demonstrations reveal the makers’ processes.

**M2:16**

Course reading: The chintz jacket and petticoat form a coordinated European dress ensemble. Following the Javanese dodot, they show Indian cotton entering distinct overseas clothing practices. Shared textile circulation therefore produces different social uses and silhouettes, rather than one uniform export style.

**M3:2**

Course reading: The Persianate World / Persian Cosmopolis discussion uses Siesta to connect a Deccani scene with a wider courtly visual culture. The following madrasa comparison extends the enquiry from painting to architecture. Persianate connection is a framework for local adaptation, not a statement that every work was made in Iran.

**M3:10**

Course reading: The Kitab-e-Nauras page and Sangeet Mahal pair a literary-musical work with an architectural setting associated with Ibrahim Adil Shah II. They continue the Sarasvati and ruler comparison from slide 9 and lead into the tambur portrait. Cultural patronage is expressed across text, image, music and building.

**M4:1**

Course reading: Vosmaer’s flowers and Vermeer’s Geographer place an oceanic argument within a vase, textile, map and globe. The still life and inhabited interior connect collected goods with geographical knowledge and pictorial skill. The subsequent VOC material makes the commercial network explicit.

**M5:2**

Course reading: The Mughal and Iranian animal carpets are placed within the question of continental and maritime trade. Their shared textile format supports comparison of animal imagery and production contexts across regions. The next muslin examples extend the enquiry from patterned furnishing to the material qualities of cloth.

**M6:3**

Course reading: The unfinished Pedana woodblocks and finished Polavaram cotton connect a carved matrix to textile printing.

 This precedes the European Saint Sebastian block-and-impression pair. The sequence compares a printing principle across supports and uses, while keeping the specific practices distinct.

**M7:6**

Course reading: Père Tanguy’s Japanese-print backdrop is followed by Sunflowers and Almond Blossoms under Van Gogh’s imagined Japan. Collecting, colour, contour and cropped plant forms offer different ways to engage Japanese imagery. Japanese influence is therefore broader than a Japanese subject or the direct copy of one print.

**M8:1**

Course reading: The Ahmedabad exhibition poster frames its title with a floral trade-textile detail. The original cloth becomes the visual identity of a contemporary exhibition about distant markets. The ensuing museum sequence examines how present displays assemble evidence for those historical connections.

**M8:3**

Course reading: The Interwoven Globe entrance banner and gallery sightline connect an exhibition’s public framing with its arrangement of textiles and images. Position, scale and the view through the gallery invite cross-object comparisons. The next Asia in Amsterdam installation provides a second curatorial method for presenting historical circulation.

**M8:6**

Course reading: The Mumbai trade-textile graphic, ROM display and Southeast Asian Ramayana textile connect contemporary curatorial framing with different uses of Indian cloth. Their sequence distinguishes an exhibition identity, an arranged group of garments and an individual ceremonial textile. Market, subject and present display are different parts of its social history.

This comparison develops the previous slide’s account of architectural combination rather than declaring the two monuments identical in structure or function.

This sequence leads from the opening palampore to named making practices. A historical map and a modern route diagram contribute different kinds of geographical evidence.

Course reading: The tambur portrait appears beneath two European prints under A travelling painting. Their arrangement invites comparison of pose, musical subject and travelling images. **M5:10**

**M5:11**

**M5:21, M5:22**

Course reading: Jahangir’s embrace of Shah Abbas uses a mapped globe and unequal figure scale for an allegory of sovereignty; the next folio places Jahangir with Jesus in separate images.

Horse trading and royal imagery | Slide Context
**M1:1**

Course reading: The cover pairs a floral ceramic dish and floral fabric with a stone trader-and-horses relief under Ebb and Flow: Art and Globalism of Oceanic Networks. Repeated flowers connect ceramic and textile; the relief contributes the people and traded animals. This cross-media grouping argues for the circulation of goods, designs and artisanal knowledge through contact. The Paigah Tombs and Coromandel kalamkari hanging on slides 2–3 extend that argument into architectural ornament, textile making and human interaction.

**M1:9, M1:10, M1:11**

Course reading: The location map, three-tiered platform and close views of carved bands develop one argument about the Mahanabami Dibba. Royal ceremony is materialized through spatial elevation and repeated scenes of animals and people. Narasimha and Chenchu Lakshmi keep religious imagery within that programme. The next tank and Rama Temple comparison asks how water, festival and monumental narrative relate.

**M1:15**

Course reading: The early granite carving and later green-chlorite facing are placed together as phases of the Mahanabami Dibba. Differences in surface, cutting and figural handling are read historically within one monument. The preceding memorial comparison supplies a stylistic reference; the following horse-trade slide shifts attention to the people and goods represented.

**M1:16**

Course reading: The trader with horses is placed beside a wootz dagger under Trade connections, with textiles named in the lecture discussion. The grouping connects traded animals, metal and cloth to royal imagery. The collar and performer comparisons on slides 17–18 extend commerce into the movement of dress and visual forms.

**M1:22**

Course reading: Vijaya Vitthala friezes, animal-bearing columns and three warrior panels extend the enquiry into interregional imagery beyond the royal platform. Compare clothing, weapons, pose and composite animals within their architectural positions. Differences among the three warriors matter: they are separate carved figures, not duplicate views of one person.

**M1:25**

Course reading: The royal platform, horse trader, hero stone and warrior recap the module’s cultural/trade argument. Ceremony, commerce, commemoration and martial imagery contribute different evidence. Their grouping joins social and political functions to travelling forms; it does not reduce Hampi’s art to one exclusively religious or decorative meaning.

**M8:20**

Course reading: The Vijaya Vitthala warrior, Ascetic Riding a Nag and Père Tanguy form the final recap. Stone carving, a marbled painting and a European portrait surrounded by Japanese prints supply three different histories of connection.

text:
Japonisme: reception and transformation | Definition and Grounded Significance
Course reading: Japonisme concerns European responses to Japanese art and objects. Artists adapted viewpoints, contours, cropping and decorative arrangements in different ways. Cassatt’s documented intaglio process and Monet’s oil painting show that influence need not mean importing the source medium unchanged.

text:
Japonisme: reception and transformation | Slide Context
**M7:1, M7:2, M7:3**

Course reading: The Great Wave, the introductory ukiyo-e image and Lake Chuzenji establish a Japanese print vocabulary of framing, flat colour, landscape and scale. They prepare the following Van Gogh–Eisen comparison. The Japanese examples remain distinct works rather than interchangeable illustrations of one national style.

**M7:4**

Course reading: Eisen’s courtesan and Van Gogh’s painted version present a direct source-and-adaptation pair. Figure and costume are retained while palette, border imagery and medium change. The next Père Tanguy portrait extends appropriation into collecting and assembling Japanese images within a European painting.

**M7:5, M7:6**

Course reading: Père Tanguy’s Japanese-print backdrop is followed by Sunflowers and Almond Blossoms under Van Gogh’s imagined Japan. Collecting, colour, contour and cropped plant forms offer different ways to engage Japanese imagery. Japanese influence is therefore broader than a Japanese subject or the direct copy of one print.

**M7:7**

Course reading: Zola’s portrait and the enlarged reproductions on its wall make artistic association visible inside an interior. Olympia, a Japanese figure and a monochrome group are objects of pictorial reference within Manet’s painting. The components connect collecting to portrait identity without becoming separately inspected original prints.

**M7:8**

Course reading: The Art Institute Water Lilies and MoMA’s multi-panel work compare related subject matter at different scales. The gallery arrangement adds seating, open floor and viewing distance to the painted surface. Compare individual works and the bodily viewing conditions rather than treating every Water Lilies image as one object.

**M7:9**

Course reading: Jane Avril and Divan Japonais place Japanese-inspired cropping and contour within Parisian entertainment publicity. Performer, spectator and instrument are organized differently in the two posters. Their subject and lithographic process remain distinct from Japanese woodblock manufacture.

**M7:10**

Course reading: La Japonaise, Cassatt’s The Letter and Mizuno’s After the Bath compare costume performance, domestic pictorial design and a Japanese print. The three illustrate different forms of Japanese reception. Cassatt’s intaglio medium remains distinct from woodblock, and Mizuno’s later print cannot be her direct source.

**M7:11**

Course reading: Hokusai’s Mannen Bridge and Monet’s Japanese bridge are paired through the bridge’s graphic curve. The populated urban crossing and garden pond have different scales, settings and media. The comparison makes a formal relation explicit without establishing that Monet copied this exact impression.
